title: When Multi-Agent Helps (and Hurts)
summary: Splitting a task across several agents is not automatically better — it adds coordination cost, latency, and new ways to fail. Multi-agent pays off when a problem has genuinely separable roles or contexts; for most tasks a single well-tooled agent is simpler, cheaper, and more reliable.

subtopics.title: Multi-agent means many loops, not one
subtopics.explanation: A single agent is one LLM loop with a set of tools; a multi-agent system is several such loops that pass messages, delegate work, or share state to reach a goal. Each extra agent is another prompt, another context window, and another point where things can drift. Recognising that you are adding whole loops — not just tools — is what frames every trade-off in this topic.
subtopics.example:
# single agent: one loop, many tools
answer = run_agent(goal, tools=[search, calc, db])

# multi-agent: several loops that talk to each other
plan = planner_agent(goal)              # loop 1
draft = writer_agent(plan)              # loop 2
final = editor_agent(draft)             # loop 3
# three prompts, three contexts, three chances to go wrong

subtopics.title: Every hop adds coordination cost
subtopics.explanation: When agents hand work to each other, each hop needs a message, a re-explanation of context, and often a re-read of prior output — extra tokens and latency the model spends just to stay in sync. This overhead grows with the number of agents and the amount of context they must share. Coordination cost is the tax you pay for splitting a task, and it is easy to underestimate.
subtopics.example:
# each handoff re-sends context the next agent needs
msg_to_writer = {
    "goal": goal,
    "plan": planner_output,        # re-sent
    "constraints": constraints,    # re-sent
}
# tokens billed again + a full extra round-trip of latency
draft = writer_agent(msg_to_writer)
# 3 agents sharing state can mean 3x the context tokens

subtopics.title: More agents means a bigger failure surface
subtopics.explanation: A single agent fails in one place; a pipeline of agents fails if any link is wrong, and errors compound as one agent's mistake becomes the next agent's input. You now have to handle partial failures, retries per agent, and disagreements between agents. The failure surface — the total set of things that can break — scales with the number of agents and the edges between them.
subtopics.example:
# error from agent A silently poisons agent B
plan = planner_agent(goal)          # returns a subtly wrong plan
draft = writer_agent(plan)          # faithfully writes the wrong thing
final = editor_agent(draft)         # polishes the wrong thing
# no single step 'failed' -> hard to detect, hard to trace
# each edge between agents is a new place to validate

subtopics.title: Split only on genuinely separable work
subtopics.explanation: Multi-agent shines when subtasks have distinct roles, tools, or contexts that barely overlap — e.g. a retrieval agent, a coding agent, and a reviewer, each with its own instructions and permissions. If the parts are tightly coupled and constantly need each other's intermediate state, splitting just multiplies the coordination cost. The test is separability: could a specialist own this piece with a clean interface?
subtopics.example:
# GOOD split: separable roles, clean interfaces
facts = research_agent(question)        # only searches
code  = coding_agent(spec, facts)       # only writes code
ok    = review_agent(code)              # only critiques

# BAD split: pieces that constantly need each other's half-done state
# (better as ONE agent than two agents ping-ponging every step)

subtopics.title: One good agent often beats many
subtopics.explanation: Before reaching for orchestration, ask whether a single agent with better tools, a sharper prompt, or a larger context window would do the job — it usually removes the coordination tax entirely. Multi-agent is a scaling and specialisation tool, not a default. Starting simple and only splitting when a real bottleneck forces it is the cheapest path to a reliable system.
subtopics.example:
# tempting: three agents for a small task
# planner -> researcher -> writer  (lots of glue, lots of tokens)

# usually better: one agent with the same tools
answer = run_agent(
    goal=goal,
    tools=[search, write_file],
    system="Plan, research, then write. Think step by step.",
)
# no handoffs, one context, far less to break

foundations.overview: A multi-agent system replaces one LLM loop with several that coordinate — by delegating, messaging, or sharing state — to solve a problem. The appeal is specialisation and parallelism: dedicated agents with their own tools, prompts, and permissions. But every added agent brings coordination cost (extra tokens and latency to keep agents in sync) and enlarges the failure surface (more links that can break, and errors that compound down a pipeline). The honest default is a single well-tooled agent; you reach for multiple agents only when a task has genuinely separable roles or contexts that a specialist can own behind a clean interface. Framed this way, multi-agent is a deliberate scaling choice with real costs, not a free upgrade — and knowing when it hurts is as important as knowing when it helps.
foundations.formalDefinition: A multi-agent system is a set of two or more LLM-driven agents, each with its own loop and possibly its own tools and instructions, that coordinate via message passing, delegation, or shared state to accomplish a task whose subgoals are distributed among them.
foundations.whyItMatters: Teams often add agents expecting quality gains and instead get slower, costlier, harder-to-debug systems. Understanding the coordination cost and failure-surface trade-offs lets you split a task only when the benefit is real, avoiding a common and expensive over-engineering trap.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of hiring. One capable generalist needs no meetings; a team of specialists can do more but must hold standups, write handoff docs, and re-explain context, and the project stalls if any one person drops the ball. Adding agents is adding headcount — sometimes worth it, never free.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Multi-agent setups appear where roles are truly distinct: a researcher plus a writer plus an editor, a planner routing to specialist coders, or parallel workers each summarising a different document before a merge step. Single-agent loops still cover the majority of production tasks.
commonUseCases: Parallel work over independent chunks (map then reduce)
Separating tool permissions or contexts for safety
Very long tasks that exceed one context window

commonMisconceptions.myth: More agents always means better results.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Each agent adds coordination cost and a new failure point; a single well-tooled agent is often more accurate, cheaper, and far easier to debug.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Multi-agent is the default architecture for anything complex.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Complexity alone doesn't justify splitting. Only genuinely separable roles or contexts do; tightly coupled subtasks are better as one loop.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Splitting a task automatically makes it faster.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Sequential handoffs add latency and re-sent context. Speedups come only from true parallelism over independent work, not from splitting per se.

checkpoints.prompt: What is the main hidden cost of splitting a task across multiple agents?
options: The model gets less accurate at math
Coordination cost: extra tokens and latency to keep agents in sync, plus a larger failure surface
You must pay for a separate API key per agent
Agents cannot use tools once there is more than one
checkpoints.explanation: Every handoff re-sends context (tokens) and adds a round-trip (latency), and each new agent and edge is another thing that can break — errors even compound down a pipeline. That coordination tax is what teams routinely underestimate.

checkpoints.prompt: Which task is the BEST candidate for a multi-agent design?
options: A pipeline where a research agent gathers facts, a coding agent writes code from them, and a reviewer critiques — each with distinct tools and instructions
Rewrite one sentence in a friendlier tone
Answer a single factual question with no tools
checkpoints.explanation: That task has genuinely separable roles with distinct tools and clean interfaces between them — the exact condition where specialisation outweighs coordination cost. The others are trivially handled by a single call or a single agent.

checkpoints.prompt: Why is this two-agent design likely worse than a single agent?
checkpoints.code:
# agent A and agent B ping-pong every step
state = start
for _ in range(20):
    state = agent_A(state)   # tweaks half the state
    state = agent_B(state)   # needs A's half to continue
# they constantly need each other's in-progress state
options: agent_A should run twice per loop
The subtasks are tightly coupled — they need each other's half-done state every step, so splitting just multiplies coordination cost with no separability benefit
You cannot loop over two agents in Python
The loop cap of 20 is too high
checkpoints.explanation: Separability is the test for splitting. Here the two agents share tightly-coupled intermediate state on every iteration, so each hop pays the coordination tax without any clean division of labour — one loop with both capabilities would be simpler and cheaper.

keyTakeaways: Multi-agent replaces one LLM loop with several — you are adding whole loops, contexts, and failure points, not just tools.
Every handoff costs tokens (re-shared context) and latency (an extra round-trip); this coordination tax scales with agent count.
More agents means a bigger failure surface: errors compound as one agent's output becomes the next agent's input.
Split only on genuinely separable roles or contexts a specialist can own behind a clean interface — not on tightly coupled work.
Default to one well-tooled agent; reach for multi-agent only when a concrete bottleneck (context, permissions, parallelism) forces it.
